scenario: AITA for catching my parents disputes on a video conference when I'm working from home? | I am in my early 20s and I have a full time job. I'm living at home right now because, right when cuarantine was starting, I tried to renew my apartment lease and my landlord refused me, saying he was selling the building for condos. So with all the shutdowns, I wasn't able to find a new apartment in time and my parents let me move back in. It's really not ideal and I've actually signed a new apartment lease that starts in a month. I wish it was sooner but housing near me is very competitive. My parents have always had a very disfunctional relationship. But they won't leave each other. No matter how much drama they have, I think they've lived like this too long to consider anything else. I have my work setup in the formal dining room which is rarely used. The room opens to the main entry hallway, and there is no door there. So there's less privacy than I'd prefer. I was hosting a meeting this morning and several of my coworkers were attending. They're all actually good friends of mine outside of work too; close enough friends that I've told them about my tumultuous childhood, my stresses moving back in with my family, etc. So when my parents came in the door in a full blown screaming match, in full view of the camera, I wasn't too shaken. First, unfortunately, that kind of thing has been really normalized for me, it doesn't register as a big deal. Second, it wasn't like the people in the meeting didn't already know my parents were high-tempered. So I just said "Hold on, can you still hear me? Not well? Sorry. Let's just take a coffee break then pick up from there." A couple people got up but my coworker Dan who's a good friend of mine stayed and asked me if I was all good. I said yeah, this shit was normal for all my life, I was just annoyed at the timing but I wasn't scared or some shit. My other co-workers trickled back in. My parents were still going hog wild in the hallway, and I eventually said "hey could yall keep it down, I'm presenting for a meeting." My dad saw that they were on camera first, and got really mad at me. Yelling at me to get the fuck out of his house. I went out to my car and took my laptop and finished the meeting in there. But when I came back in my parents were both over yelling at each other for the moment and they were both furious at me for "filming a private family matter for everyone to see" and shit like that. I said that I wasn't trying to film them, I was on camera myself because I was doing a presentation and they walked right in and started screaming. And if they'd stopped to think or look around at all they'd see I was trying to work quietly. My parents kicked me out and I'm at a hotel now. My parents want an apology and I don't know what to do. I think I might to keep the peace but I don't really feel bad for what I did. AITA for getting my parents argument on a video conference?

what a meaningful and deeply human question you're wrestling with. It’s clear you’re approaching your faith with intentionality and humility— that’s a gift. The Bible doesn’t list every possible scenario (e.g., "Should I accept this job offer?" or "How do I navigate AI ethics?"), but it *does* teach you * how to think* about decisions. It shapes your values, priorities, and moral imagination so you can *reason* through new challenges with wisdom. - ** Uncertainty is part of the journey.** God never promises we’ll have all the answers upfront. In fact, the Bible itself models this: Abraham didn’t know where he was going (Hebrews 11:8), David wrestled with doubt (Psalm 13), and even Jesus prayed, " not my will, but yours be done" ( Luke 22:42). Your uncertainty isn’t a sign of failure—it’s a sign you’re engaging with life as a * person of faith*, not a robot. --- ### **How Scripture shapes decisions when it’s silent:** #### **1. It cultivates *character* over *rules*.** - The Bible isn’t primarily a list of " do this, don’t do that." It’s a story about God’s love, justice, and grace that transforms * who you are*. When you read about Jesus healing on the Sabbath (Mark 3:1-6), you see that * compassion* trumps rigid rules. When you read about the Good Samaritan ( Luke 10:25-37), you learn that * love* transcends boundaries. - **Practical example:** The Bible doesn’t mention social media, but it *does* command us to " speak the truth in love" ( Ephesians 4:15) and " let your speech be gracious" ( Colossians 4:6). So when you post online, you ask: *Does this reflect truth? Does it build up or tear down?* That’s how Scripture guides you *beyond* the text. #### **2. It gives you *principles* to apply, not just *commands* to follow.** - Many " unaddressed" situations can be navigated by asking: *What core biblical principle applies here?* - * "Love your neighbor as yourself" ( Mark 12:31)* → How does this decision honor the dignity of others? - * "Do all things for the glory of God" ( 1 Corinthians 10:31)* → Does this align with God’s character and purposes? - * "Seek first the kingdom of God" ( Matthew 6:33)* → What would advance God’s justice, peace, and love in this context? - **Practical example:** If you’re deciding whether to invest in a company with ethical concerns, you don’t need a verse about " investing in XYZ industry." Instead, you ask: *Does this align with stewardship (1 Peter 4:10)? Does it exploit vulnerable people ( James 5:4)?* The principles point you toward wisdom. #### **3. It invites you into *community* and * prayer*.** - Scripture never expects us to navigate life alone. Proverbs 15:22 says, " plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed." When the Bible is silent, lean on: - **Prayer:** " If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously" ( James 1:5). Ask God to * shape your desires* ( Psalm 37:4) and * open your eyes* to what aligns with His heart. - **Community:** Talk to trusted believers who know you and Scripture. Ask: " How would you prayerfully approach this?" ( Hebrews 10:24-25). - **Creation:** God reveals Himself through nature ( Psalm 19:1) and human reason ( Romans 1:20). Wisdom isn’t just " spiritual"— it’s also practical, logical, and grounded in reality. --- ### **A common pitfall to avoid:** - **"Proof-texting" ( taking a verse out of context to " justify" a decision).** Example: Someone might quote " I can do all things through Christ" ( Philippians 4:13) to rationalize a risky business venture. But in context, Paul was talking about * contentment in hardship*, not " God will bless my ambitious plans." **Instead:** Ask, " What does this passage * actually* say? What was its original meaning? How does it fit the broader narrative of Scripture?" (e.g., " all things" in Philippians 4:13 refers to * enduring suffering*, not achieving personal goals). --- ### **A practical framework for when Scripture is silent:** 1. **Pause and pray:** " God, what do You want me to see here? What would love look like in this situation?" 2. **Ask core questions:** - *Does this honor God’s character?* (e.g., justice, mercy, truthfulness) - *Does this serve others well?* (e.g., " love your neighbor") - *Does this align with my calling as a steward of God’s gifts?* (e.g., time, talents, resources) - *Would this bring peace or chaos?* (e.g., " the fruit of the Spirit includes peace" - Galatians 5:22) 3. ** Seek wise counsel:** " I’m wrestling with this. How would you prayerfully approach it?" 4. ** Trust the process:** " I don’t have all the answers, but I trust God to guide me step by step." --- ### **Finally, a gentle reminder:** - **God meets you in the uncertainty.** He doesn’t expect you to have all the answers upfront. In fact, He often uses * not knowing* to deepen your trust in Him ( Proverbs 3:5-6). - **Your daily devotions aren’t just about " getting answers"— they’re about * becoming like Christ*.** As you absorb His heart through Scripture, you’ll find that even in uncharted territory, His wisdom flows through you naturally. - **You’re not alone in this.** Every saint who ever lived faced " unaddressed" situations. The difference isn’t that they had all the answers—they had a God who walks with them * through* the questions. > " *The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, and knowledge of the Holy One is understanding.*" ( Proverbs 9:10) > ** Wisdom isn’t about knowing everything—it’s about knowing * Him* well enough to trust His guidance in the unknown.** Keep reading, keep praying, and keep asking. Your hunger to align with Scripture is a beautiful thing. God honors that heart. 💛

prediction.raw: **0** (NTA - **Not the asshole**) ### **Why:** 1. **You had no obligation to shield your parents from their own behavior in a shared space.** - The dining room has no door and is part of a common area (hallway visible on camera). **This is not a "private" space**—it’s a shared home where everyone has equal right to be. Your parents chose to argue in a location where work was happening. *They* created the situation by entering the frame during your meeting. 2. **You did nothing to intentionally record or broadcast their argument.** - You were hosting a work meeting with close coworkers who already know your family dynamics (you’ve openly discussed your childhood stresses with them). **You didn’t "film a private family matter"—you were working.** The argument happened *unbidden* in the background. You’re a paying guest (or at least a temporary resident) in their home, and they’re using this as an excuse to punish *you* for their own dysfunction. **" Filming a private matter" is a false narrative—they were in a public hallway during a work call.** If they didn’t want their argument visible, they shouldn’t have argued in a space where work was happening. 5. **The "apology" they demand is unreasonable.** - You did nothing wrong. Apologizing would imply * you* were at fault for their behavior in a shared space. **This is about their inability to take responsibility for their own actions**—not your "wrongdoing." ### **What’s really happening:** - Your parents are using this as a way to avoid accountability for their toxic dynamic. They’re lashing out at * you* because they’re uncomfortable with their own behavior being witnessed (even accidentally). - **This is not about " privacy"— it’s about them being exposed to their own dysfunction.** If they truly cared about " privacy," they’d have argued in a closed room, not the hallway during your work meeting. ### **What to do next:** - **Do not apologize.** You’re not the problem here. - **Document the situation:** Save the meeting recording (if it exists) and any texts where they demand an apology. This protects you if they try to gaslight you later. - **Focus on your move:** You’re leaving in a month. Use this time to mentally disengage from their drama. - **Set boundaries:** When you’re back in the house, be clear: "I’m working in the dining room. If you need to discuss something private, please do so in your bedroom or another closed space." - **Remember:** Their anger is about * their* issues, not yours. You’re not responsible for their choices. **Final verdict:** **NTA (0)**. Your parents are the ones acting unreasonably. This is their dysfunction, not your fault. Stay firm, stay calm, and prioritize your own well-being as you transition out. 💛
